claims.text: Substituting a significant fraction of higher-density elements with low-density elements such as Al or Ti reduces the overall density of lightweight high-entropy alloys.
Increasing low-density-element content and optimizing cooling rates promotes a stable high-entropy matrix containing ultrafine precipitates.
A high-entropy matrix containing ultrafine precipitates enhances mechanical strength.
A high-entropy matrix containing ultrafine precipitates enhances corrosion resistance.
A high-entropy matrix containing ultrafine precipitates enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Ultrafine precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation movement.
Controlled cooling refines the alloy microstructure.
The resulting precipitates mitigate phase instability and limit degradation pathways in corrosive and high-temperature oxidizing environments.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the tailored alloy will have significantly lower density.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the tailored alloy will maintain or improve mechanical strength.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the tailored alloy will exhibit improved corrosion resistance.
Relative to the baseline alloy, the tailored alloy will exhibit improved high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Failure to optimize the cooling rate will prevent formation of the superior microstructure and abolish the predicted benefits.
Exceeding a critical low-density-element concentration can cause phase separation or brittle intermetallic formation and abolish the predicted benefits.
Preliminary literature supports the proposed effects of composition tailoring and cooling-rate optimization.
